questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Sum and Product of Eigenvalues of a 2x2 Matrix
questions.problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{7}{5} & -2\end{aligned}],$ find the product of the eigenvalues of $A.$
questions.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2}=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the determinant of $A.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} & =det(A) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{7}{5} & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-2)-\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{7}{5} \\  & =-1-\frac{7}{2} \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing the Inverse of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Its Powers
questions.problem: If $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -3 & 0 \\ 7 & -5 & -1\end{aligned}],$ then ${A}^{-1}=$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -3-\lambda  & 0 \\ 7 & -5 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ -1 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )((2-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )+1) & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -5) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}+2{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda -5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3}+2{A}^{2}-4A-5I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{3}+2{A}^{2}-4A-5I) & =O \\ {A}^{2}+2A-4I-5{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =-\frac{4}{5}I+\frac{2}{5}A+\frac{1}{5}{A}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing the Inverse of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Its Powers
questions.problem: Given that $\,A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value $p+q.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-8A+6I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-8A+6I) & =O \\ A-8I+6{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 6{A}^{-1} & =8I-A \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{4}{3}I-\frac{1}{6}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{4}{3},$ $q=-\frac{1}{6}$ and

$$
p+q=\frac{4}{3}+(-\frac{1}{6})=\frac{7}{6}.
$$

$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{8}{9},$ $q=-\frac{1}{9},$ and 

$$
p+q=\frac{8}{9}+(-\frac{1}{9})=\frac{7}{9}.

questions.problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}],$ and ${A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value of $p+q.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 4 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-8 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-5A-2 & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-5A-2) & ={A}^{-1}O \\ A-5I-2{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =-\frac{5}{2}I+\frac{1}{2}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-\frac{5}{2},$ $q=\frac{1}{2}$ and

$$
p+q=-\frac{5}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=-2.
$$

questions.problem: If $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ with characteristic polynomial $p(x)={x}^{2}-x-20,$ then ${A}^{3}=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's divide the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{3}$ by characteristic polynomial $p(x)={x}^{2}-x-20,$ using long division:

|  | $\,\,x$ | $+$ | $1$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${x}^{2}-x-20\,$ | $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{3}\,\,}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  | ${x}^{3}$ | $-$ | ${x}^{2}$ | $-$ | $20x$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  | ${x}^{2}$ | $+$ | $20x$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  | ${x}^{2}$ | $-$ | $x$ | $-$ | $20$ |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  | $21x$ | $+$ | $20$ |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we can write ${x}^{3}$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3} & =q(x)p(x)+(21x+20),\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)=x+1.$  Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
{A}^{3}=q(A)p(A)+(21A+20I).
$$

Now, according to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3} & =q(A)p(A)+(21A+20I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(21A+20I) \\  & =21A+20I.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given the matrix
$\,A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 10 & -5\end{aligned}]$
and $f(x)={x}^{23}-25{x}^{21}-4x+2$, find $f(A).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 0 \\ 10 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(5-\lambda )(-5-\lambda ) \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-25\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

|  | $\,\,{x}^{21}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${x}^{2}-25\,$ | $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{23}\,-\,25{x}^{21}\,-\,4x\,+\,2}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  | ${x}^{23}$ | $-$ | $25{x}^{21}$ |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  | $-$ | $4x$ | $+$ | $2$ |

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\  & =q(x)p(x)+(-4x+2)\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)={x}^{21}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(-4A+2I).
$$

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(-4A+2I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(-4A+2I) \\  & =-4A+2I \\  & =-4[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 10 & -5\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-20 & 0 \\ -40 & 20\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-18 & 0 \\ -40 & 22\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:

$\,A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 12 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]$
and $f(x)={x}^{21}-16{x}^{19}+6x-3$, find $f(A).$

Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 12 \\ 0 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda ) \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-16\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

|  | $\,\,{x}^{19}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${x}^{2}-16\,$ | $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{21}\,-\,16{x}^{19}\,+\,6x\,\,-\,\,3}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  | ${x}^{21}$ | $-$ | $16{x}^{19}$ |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  | $6x$ | $-$ | $3$ |

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\  & =q(x)p(x)+(6x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)={x}^{19}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(6A-3I).
$$

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(6A-3I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(6A-3I) \\  & =6A-3I \\  & =6[\begin{aligned}4 & 12 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}24 & 72 \\ 0 & -24\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}21 & 72 \\ 0 & -27\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

|  | $\,\,{x}^{14}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${x}^{2}-4\,$ | $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{16}\,-\,4{x}^{14}\,+\,7x\,-\,3}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  | ${x}^{16}$ | $-$ | $4{x}^{14}$ |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  | $7x$ | $-$ | $3$ |

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\  & =q(x)p(x)+(7x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)={x}^{14}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I).
$$

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(7A-3I) \\  & =7A-3I \\  & =7[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 14 \\ -42 & -28\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 14 \\ -42 & -31\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.problem: Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix such that $\textrm{tr}(A)=-4$ and $\textrm{det}(A)=-18.$ If $A^2 = xA + yI$ for constants $x$ and $y,$ then find the value of $x+y.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by 

$$
p(\lambda)=\lambda^2-\textrm{tr}(A)\lambda+\textrm{det}(A).
$$

Therefore, using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p(A) & =O \\ {A}^{2}-\text{tr}(A)A+\text{det}(A)I & =O \\ {A}^{2} & =\text{tr}(A)A-\text{det}(A)I \\ {A}^{2} & =-4A+18I.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x+y = -4+18 = 14.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Expressing the Inverse of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Its Powers
canonical_examples.problem: Given that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14058184/assets/b2240a11f1760050914a9c02554e0b7e86cd84d420fb437a43d95b474103b26c.png) and $A^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value of $p+q.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\textrm{det}(A-\lambda I)=0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-8-\lambda  & -9 \\ 6 & 7-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-8-\lambda )(7-\lambda )+54 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}+A-2I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by $A^{-1}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}+A-2I) & =O \\ A+I-2{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{1}{2}I\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\dfrac{1}{2},$ $q=\dfrac{1}{2},$ and 

$$
p+q=\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}=1.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & -5 \\ 3 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )+15 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

|  | $\:\:x^{10}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x^2-1\:$ | $\!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{x^{12} \, - \, x^{10}  +  2x  -  1 {\phantom{|}} }$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  | $x^{12}$ | $-$ | $x^{10}$ |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  | $2x$ | $-$ | $1$ |

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\  & ={x}^{10}({x}^{2}-1)+(2x-1),\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x) = x^{10}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A) = q(A)p(A)+(2A-I).
$$

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(2A-I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(2A-I) \\  & =2A-I \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}4 & -5 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -10 \\ 6 & -8\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -10 \\ 6 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
